prose.en: All the time that you use this book, we advise you to keep a personal vocabulary notebook. There is no one correct way to organise a vocabulary notebook, but it is a good idea to think about possible ways of doing so. This unit gives some possibilities and examples.

Try dividing your notebook into different broad sections, with sections for words for feelings, words to describe places, words for movement, words for thinking, etc. In each section you can build families of words related in meaning, using some of the ways suggested in this unit.
Words that can be grouped under a heading or a more general word can be drawn as a tree-diagram. (See also Unit 2.)
The dotted lines mean that you can add more words to the tree as you meet them. A bubble network is also useful, since you can make it grow in whatever direction you want it to. (See Unit 2.)
A Spanish learner of English, Angeles, gave us an interview on how she marks word-class in her personal notebook. This is what she said:

'What I have just started doing is to write them depending on if they are verbs or nouns or adjectives or phrases. If they are phrases I write them in red and also the definition. If they are verbs, in black, and blue if they are nouns ... And if I write the Spanish translation I write it in another colour, so it's easy to see ... I draw some pictures too.'
When you find a synonym or an antonym of a word you already have in your book, enter it next to that word.
stop = cease ('cease' is more formal than 'stop')    urban ≠ rural

note: Left page contains full presentation prose (intro, section explanations, quoted learner interview, synonym/antonym examples); right page is exercises only and was excluded.
